113-the-secret-garden:
Mary Lennox, spoiled and lonely after her parents die in India, arrives at a gloomy Yorkshire manor. Frances Hodgson Burnett's Secret Garden follows Mary as she finds a locked garden and a hidden cousin. Martha the maid and Dickon, who talks to animals, guide her.

Mary and Dickon revive the garden in secret, and Colin, long kept indoors, learns to walk and hope. The robin, the key, and the seasons mark their growth. Magic here means fresh air, work, and kindness rather than spells. The novel became a beloved children's classic.
19889-naughty-miss-bunny-a-story-for-lit:
Naughty Miss Bunny is a story for little children by Clara Mulholland. Miss Bunny longs to be jolly, her papa's word for happy. Grown voices keep telling her to sit still. They warn her not to dirty her pretty white frock. Big people, she thinks, can do what they like. Children must do everything they are told. Her dainty sash will not survive her plans.

Mulholland wrote many tales for Catholic children. A bunny in a frock lets her preach by laughter. The comedy turns on the gap between orders and urges. Every small reader knows that gap well. Illustrations carry much of the fun in such books. The story is a period nursery piece, gentle and sly.
20009-ixion-in-heaven:
Ixion in Heaven is Disraeli's satirical tale of a mortal guest on Olympus. Ixion, a wanderer, calls Jove his only friend at its opening. But for the porch of Jove's temple, this night would finish him, he says. His loving wife and dutiful subjects have ruined him below. Olympus receives him with divine politeness and godly gossip. The mythic Ixion loved Hera; Disraeli's loves society.

The tale first appeared inside The Young Duke in 1831. Its heaven is a London salon with thunderbolts. Gods intrigue, flirt, and talk politics like Regency beaux. Disraeli's classical satire is light but pointed. Earthly ambition looks sillier from Olympus, which is the joke. The piece shows his earliest manner at its most playful.
20052-we-ten:
Barbara Yechton published We Ten, also called The Story of the Roses, in 1896. Ten young people form the close group at the heart of the tale. When Felix cannot go to college, the rest feel his loss keenly. Six of them hold a council in the schoolroom that same day.

Felix bars the four youngest from that council, calling them mere kids. That small slight shows the group's ranks and bonds at once. The story follows friends who share joys, plans, and setbacks. Readers get a warm tale of youth, loyalty, and growing up together.
20362-girls-and-women:
Girls and Women, from 1890, is a novel of a woman's narrowed life after school. A sensitive woman finds much that is mortifying in her position. All her Greek and Italian books lie packed away from use. She knows no more of science than when she left school.

At odd minutes she reads good novels, and that is all. Literature, for her, ends there, in scraps of stolen time. Novels of this era protest the waste of women's trained minds. Readers get a quiet, pointed tale of talent stifled by custom and home.
20469-ballads-of-romance-and-chivalry-po:
Ballads of Romance and Chivalry gathers popular ballads of the olden time: knights, ladies, quests, and brave deeds in verse. It belongs to a series that reprinted the old singing poetry of Britain. The editor chose pieces for story and swing, not for rarity alone.

In the preface, the editor jokes that there is no end of making selections of ballads. As a subject, they seem only less popular than Shakespeare, and every year brings a fresh output. He also warns against the new habit of confusing old ballads with modern imitations. The book keeps the true old strain apart.
20644-the-book-of-hallowe-en:
Ruth Edna Kelley's The Book of Hallowe'en traces the festival from pagan fires to American parties. It follows the night through Celts, Romans, and the church calendar. Charms, games, and ghost lore from many countries fill its chapters.

Ask a pagan of the old world for his greatest gods, the book begins, and the sun god would surely stand among them. A Greek would call him Apollo, an Egyptian Horus or Osiris, a Norseman Sol, and a Peruvian by another name. From such sun worship, Kelley builds the case for Halloween's deep roots.
20746-the-home-or-life-in-sweden:
June sun fills a large, cheerful room as The Home, or Life in Sweden, begins. A white damask cloth covers a long table set with a fine coffee service. A judge comes to breakfast with a troubled face that soon clears.

Domestic scenes carry this tale of Swedish home life in translation. Family talk, meals, and manners show a world both like and unlike the reader's own. Fredrika Bremer made home life a serious subject. Her work shaped the domestic novel across Europe and America. The book is a novel of home life in Sweden.
20753-the-wonder-island-boys-the-tribesm:
Two tribes clash in The Wonder Island Boys: The Tribesmen, a boys' adventure tale. A wagon serves as a fort as one side falls back to a stream shore. The beaten party takes cover behind it while the winners press the attack.

Castaway boys watch, learn, and step into island dangers as the tale moves. Invention, hunting, and native wars fill the Wonder Island set of books. Such tales fed boys' hunger for wild places and bold deeds. The plain, fast style keeps scenes short and clear, with a new scrape or wonder waiting in nearly every chapter.
20877-mother-west-wind-s-children:
Danny Meadow Mouse watches Mother West Wind's children, the Merry Little Breezes, at play. Thornton W. Burgess opens his 1911 tale by the Smiling Pool and Green Meadows. Sammy Jay, on a fence post, feigns a sun bath while plotting fresh mischief.

Burgess built a beloved world of talking beasts for young readers. Each tale slips in lore of real habits, haunts, and seasons. Peter Rabbit and his kin star across the long set of books. Mother West Wind's Children stands near the start of that world, warm, sly, and perfectly made for bedtime reading aloud.
21041-seen-and-unseen:
A father's last illness held no special mark for E. Katharine Bates, she writes in Seen and Unseen. Servants were banned from hinting that he lay in true danger. Nurse, brother, and godmother kept that grave watch in a hushed house.

Bates, a poet and traveller, turns from memoir to the unseen world of spirits. Ghosts, presentiments, and survival after death fill her grave inquiry here. She writes as a witness, not a scoffer, weighing tales with care. The book shows the keen interwar hunger for proof that love and mind outlast the body's brief, frail house.
21230-susan-a-story-for-children:
Amy Walton wrote this story for younger children, around eleven or twelve years old. Susan lives in London, but her ten-year-old brother is bedridden with a lasting illness. Doctors advise a warmer climate for the winter, so their mother takes him to Algiers.

Susan goes instead to her great-aunt at Ramsgate, a small seaside town in Kent. Other girls are staying there too, including Sophia Jane, Susan's age, whose behaviour seems difficult at first. The two girls learn to see each other better, and Susan learns she is not faultless herself. A French brother and sister add a second thread to the Ramsgate holiday.
21231-penelope-and-the-others-story-of-f:
Penelope Hawthorne sits in the schoolroom window at Easney Vicarage, planning gravely for her brothers and sisters, in Amy Walton's story of five country children. The book continues The Hawthorns, following the same household. Penelope, called Pennie, is famous for her plans, part from her own head and part from books.

New faces join the village world: eccentric Miss Barnicroft and poor Kettles from the cathedral city of Nearminster. Learned Dr Budge also joins, teaching one boy Latin and keeping a pet jackdaw. The Dean's daughter Sabine matches Pennie in age. Country childhood, kindness to the poor, and family scrapes fill the sequel.
21232-the-hawthorns-a-story-about-childr:
An old pear tree grows close to the nursery window at Easney Vicarage. Ivy hugs its trunk, its blossom is white each spring, and its pears drop with a soft splosh. Amy Walton opens her story of the Hawthorn children under that tree. Four of them, Penelope, Ambrose, Nancy, and David, are schoolroom children when the tale begins.

Walton wrote the book for girls of about eleven or twelve, in a late Victorian country setting. Daily life at the vicarage, lessons, games, and small troubles make the plot rather than great events. Its sequel, Penelope and the Others, continues the same family's story at Easney.
21293-brownsmith-s-boy-a-romance-in-a-ga:
George Manville Fenn sets this romance in a market garden around 1835, where fruit and vegetables are raised for daily trips to London market. Grant Dennison lives with his mother in a house overlooking the garden. After her death, old Brownsmith takes the boy in to learn the gardener's skills.

Another boy, Shock, sleeps rough around the garden, living on snails, hedgehogs, and rabbits, and teases Grant at every chance. Fenn, a keen naturalist, teaches real market gardening inside the story. Lessons run from sowing to the night cart ride to market with old Ike and the horse Basket. Danger and near disaster season the lessons, as Fenn readers expected.
21565-the-queen-s-matrimonial-ladder-a-n:
William Hone attacks King George the Fourth in The Queen's Matrimonial Ladder, a satire of 1820. Fourteen step scenes, with verses and cuts by Cruikshank, climb the ladder of Queen Caroline's wrongs. The pamphlet and its toy sold together for one shilling.

Hone, who wrote The Political House That Jack Built, reached a twenty-first edition with this piece. The king's bid to shed his wife, bag of charges and all, is mocked scene by scene. A line from Measure for Measure fronts the work. The piece shows how cheap print and bold pictures could shake a throne in Regency London.
21741-the-island-queen:
An open boat drifts on a calm Southern Ocean at the start of this Ballantyne tale of fire and water. An albatross circles the silent craft, puzzled by its stillness. In the boat, a young girl lies faint while a man struggles up to scan her face with fear. How they came there is the story's first question.

Ballantyne calls the tale the story of a queen dethroned by fire and water. Shipwreck, island life, and rule among castaways follow from that drifting boat. The sea gives and takes in his usual measure. It is a South Seas adventure built on survival, with a girl's fate at the heart of the storm and the calm.
21777-the-years-between:
Poems written across the years of the Great War make up Rudyard Kipling's The Years Between, first published in 1919. The title names the span between the old peace and whatever would follow the war. Contents range from The Declaration of London and For All We Have and Are to Epitaphs and The Female of the Species. A dedication to seven watchmen opens the book.

Kipling writes of France, of Lord Roberts, of Irish Guards, of Mesopotamia, and of sons who would not come home. Some poems scold Parliament and the public; others grieve in a few hard lines. The voice is the famous one, turned to wartime Britain. Few books show so plainly what those years asked of, and took from, his generation.
21838-which-or-between-two-women:
Two women love one man in Which? Or, Between Two Women, a French novel by Ernest Daudet in Laura E. Kendall's English translation. The tale opens with a gypsy mother fleeing with her child and dying at the Château de Chamondrin. The friendless little one is taken in and raised there. From that start, the publisher promises, stirring incidents crowd every chapter.

Paris and the country share the scene, and part of the action passes in the Conciergerie, the grim prison of the Revolution. History and fiction are woven close in this double love story. Daudet, brother of Alphonse, was among France's most read novelists. The romance keeps its grip by heart and event in equal measure, page after page.
21850-a-little-norsk-or-ol-pap-s-flaxen:
A Norwegian child grows up on the hard northern plains in Hamlin Garland's A Little Norsk, also called Ol' Pap's Flaxen, published in 1892. The book opens with a poem of the prairie winter: a cabin cowering in the blast, snow hissing like wolves across the plain. Against that cold, Garland sets the tale of a flaxen-haired girl and the old man who raises her.

Her adoptive parents, her first trip in a blizzard, and the life of a settler's cabin fill the early chapters. Garland had won fame with Main Traveled Roads for his true pictures of farm life. This shorter tale brings the same honesty to a child's story. The plains are beautiful and pitiless in his telling, and both shape the girl.
21930-salthaven:
A ship-owner's son comes home to the firm in W. W. Jacobs's Salthaven, a novel of 1908. Mr. John Vyner tells his chief clerk Hartley that young Robert will join the firm next week. Robert has had three years at Cambridge and two studying business methods round the world. Hartley must give up his room, for a time, Vyner says, with kindly condescension. The general office is cheerful, too, he suggests.

Jacobs builds his comedy on such small demotions and the hopes tied to them. Salthaven port life, clerks, sailors, and courtship fill the chapters. His touch is lighter than the satire it hides. The novel shows Jacobs stretching his Thames-side world into a full social comedy, where a room with a door can decide a man's worth.
22096-stories-the-iroquois-tell-their-ch:
Mabel Powers collected Stories the Iroquois Tell Their Children in 1917. Powers lived near the Iroquois and learned their tales from tribal storytellers. She pictures the winter fire, where the children cry "Heh" and crowd close. The storyteller then begins, and ends each tale with "Na ho" — it is the end.

The stories tell of the Little People, of trees, flowers, birds, and animals. They explain how things came to be and how children should behave. Powers wrote them down in simple English for young readers. Her book keeps a place among the gentler records of Iroquois oral tradition made in the early twentieth century.
22156-the-boy-with-the-u-s-weather-men:
Francis Rolt-Wheeler put his boy hero with the United States Weather Bureau in The Boy with the U.S. Weather Men, issued in 1917. Rolt-Wheeler's U.S. Service series sent boys inside real government work. This volume opens in a storm: Ross looks down at his Airedale, soaked to a seal's likeness, tugging at his trouser leg. The boy is every bit as wet as the dog.

From that drenching the story follows forecasting, storm warnings, and mountain observatories. Weather men read instruments, telegraph warnings, and save ships and harvests by minutes. Rolt-Wheeler packs in real science between adventures. His series made civil servants into heroes for boy readers.
22175-stories-from-the-ballads-told-to-t:
Mary MacGregor retold Stories from the Ballads Told to the Children, with pictures by Katharine Cameron. MacGregor found the tales in old books of song. She promises children songs of love and hate, of joy and sorrow. When they are older, she hopes, they will seek the same old books themselves.

Her prose turns famous ballads into clear stories for young readers. Carterhaugh's lone plain, where Tam Lin waited, sets one scene. Others tell of Robin Hood's world, fairy queens, and true lovers parted by feud. The book belongs to a series that carried Britain's classics to the nursery, and its ballads carry blood, magic, and music in softened form.
22372-a-labrador-doctor-the-autobiograph:
A Labrador Doctor is the autobiography of Wilfred Thomason Grenfell, published in 1919. Grenfell served as a medical missionary in Labrador. He admits he long resisted pressure from friends to write his life.

Living alongside his own autobiography felt risky to him. It calls, he says, for confessions from its author. In God's eyes, the only alternative is a book of lies. That blunt honesty frames everything that follows in the memoir. Readers get a doctor's years among fishing folk in a harsh north. The book made Labrador's needs known to a wide world of readers.
22728-the-foundations-of-the-origin-of-s:
Charles Darwin wrote the two essays gathered here in 1842 and 1844, the first drafts of his theory of evolution. The catalog record gives no year for this edition. Long before On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859, Darwin sketched his ideas in private, testing them against the evidence of breeding and geology.

The contents of the 1844 essay show the theory already formed. Variation, its causes, and its hereditary tendency come first. Then come selection, the crossing of breeds, and the descent of domestic races from wild stocks. Darwin weighs the limits of variation and sums up what domestication proves. His son Francis later published these foundations so readers could watch the great argument grow. Few books let us see a world-changing idea at the drafting stage so plainly.
22888-under-the-window-pictures-rhymes-f:
Kate Greenaway fills Under the Window with pictures and rhymes for children. One verse sends three tabbies out with their cats to tea. Each cat takes a favorite seat, calls politely for milk, and settles down purring. A riddle closes the verse, asking young readers to count up the cats' lives.

Greenaway's children wear the quaint dress that made her books famous across England and America. Short poems, games, and everyday scenes fill the pages, all carried by her drawings. The book first charmed Victorian nurseries and never really left them. Modern readers meet it as a landmark of children's publishing, gentle in tone and exact in dress, manners, and small pleasures.
22896-little-stories-for-little-children:
Plain lessons wear story dress in Little Stories for Little Children. One day a poor girl came to Ann, asking for bread, since she had eaten none all day. Ann had no bread to give. Instead she handed over the sixpence her mother had given her, telling the girl to buy bread with it.

Short tales like Ann's fill the little book, each built to teach kindness, honesty, or obedience without a long sermon. The language stays simple enough for new readers sounding out words. Such books were the first rung of the reading ladder in their day. They still show how early children's publishing worked, a story, a virtue, and a page a small reader could finish alone.
22922-the-posy-ring-a-book-of-verse-for-:
Editors Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Archibald Smith gather children's verse in The Posy Ring, published in 1903. Its acknowledgments thank publishers for reprint rights, naming poems like Baby Corn, Susan Hartley Swett's The Blue Jay, and John B. Tabb's Fern Song, A Bunch of Roses, and The Child at Bethlehem.

A posy ring was a ring carrying a verse inside the band, and the editors chose the name for a circle of poems. The anthology mixes nursery rhymes, nature verse, and short lyrics meant for reading aloud at home and school. Many selections became standards of the American classroom. The book preserves the taste of its moment, when a good anthology was a family's poetry shelf in one volume.
23189-the-lily-of-leyden:
The Lily of Leyden is a work of historical fiction set in the Dutch town of Leyden. High above the town rises an ancient tower, commonly linked by local belief to Hengist and to the Saxon crossing from Holland into Britain. Few spots nearby stand anywhere near as high.

Mynheer Van der Werf and a young woman named Jaqueline climb the mound to that tower. They mount a flight of winding steps to the battlements at the top. From there the whole district opens below them. Readers get Dutch history, old legend, and a wide view joined in one scene.
319-the-ways-of-men:
Eliot Gregory, writing as An Idler, studies American society with a light, knowing pen. The Ways of Men, from the 1900 Scribner's edition, is dedicated to Edith Wharton, who praised the author. Its first chapter, Uncle Sam, traces pompous classical town names.

A cultured governor named embryo towns Utica, Syracuse, and Ithaca, and Gregory notes the comic gap between name and place. Later chapters tour manners, money, and travel in the Gilded Age. The Merrymount Press printing adds typographic charm. The book suits readers of Wharton and James. Gregory's idle essays pair with Wharton's novels of the same society.
473-stories-to-tell-to-children:
Sara Cone Bryant gathers fifty-three tales for telling aloud in this companion to her guide on storytelling. The Little Red Hen, the Gingerbread Man, the Boy Who Cried Wolf, the Elves and the Shoemaker, and David and Goliath sit beside lesser-known tales from many lands. Notes for the teller open the book.

Bryant shapes each tale for voice, not print, with short sentences and clear action. Stories suit school, home, and library hours. The volume remains a handy store for tellers who want tried tales that hold small listeners from first line to last.
514-little-women:
Louisa May Alcott follows the four March sisters through Civil War years and beyond in this beloved novel. Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy live in modest Concord with their mother while their father serves as chaplain. Christmas without gifts, plays, picnics, and neighbor Laurie fill part one; weddings, work, and loss fill part two.

Alcott writes with warmth, humor, and plain moral sense, letting Jo's pen and Beth's music carry the heart. The book grew from Alcott's own family life, yet it speaks to any home. It endures as a classic of girlhood, where love, work, and pluck shape four very different lives.
677-the-heroes-or-greek-fairy-tales-for-:
Charles Kingsley retold three Greek myths for young readers: the tales of Perseus, Jason and the Golden Fleece, and Theseus. He keeps the gods, monsters, and sea voyages of the old stories, but tells them in a plain, warm voice meant for children at home. Each hero faces a hard task and must show courage, patience, and care for others.

Perseus sets out against the Gorgon, Jason sails with the Argonauts in search of the fleece, and Theseus meets the Minotaur in the maze. Kingsley frames the myths as lessons in how to act well, not just as wonders. The book has lasted as a first door into Greek myth, because it keeps the adventure while making the old tales easy to follow.
681-creatures-that-once-were-men:
Maxim Gorky gathered stories of men who had fallen out of settled life in late Tsarist Russia: tramps, thieves, and drifters living on the edge of towns and ports. They were once workers, soldiers, or clerks, but drink, debt, or bad luck cut them loose. Gorky knew this world at first hand and wrote it without softening its dirt or its hunger.

The tales turn on small choices: a job refused, a coin stolen, a kindness given or withheld. Beneath the rough talk, the men still argue about God, freedom, and what a human life is worth. The book made Gorky's name as the voice of Russia's outcasts, and it still hits hard as a portrait of pride and ruin among people the world had passed by.
908-treatise-on-parents-and-children:
George Bernard Shaw wrote this treatise on the relations of parents and children, with essays on trailing clouds of glory, the child as father to the man, and what a child is. He tackles the sin of Nadab and Abihu, the making of monsters, small and large families, and children as nuisances, child fanciers, and childhood as a state of sin.

Shaw argues, with wit and provocation, that children are persons, not property, and that schools and homes often crush what they claim to nurture. His prose is brisk, combative, and full of paradox. The book is a bracing Shaw manifesto, and it still challenges readers who think children should be seen and not heard.
918-sketches-of-young-gentlemen:
Charles Dickens, as Boz, sketched young gentlemen for the young ladies of Great Britain, Ireland, Wales, and the Channel Islands, to whom the volume is humbly dedicated. He parades the dandy, the bashful youth, the military aspirant, and other types, each with his dress, talk, and airs.

Dickens writes with satirical affection, catching the vanities and hopes of young men on the town. His sketches are short, vivid, and theatrical, full of London shops, balls, and lodgings. The volume pairs with his sketches of young couples, and it charms readers who enjoy social comedy in miniature.
96-the-monster-men:
A scientist on a Borneo island grows men in vats, and one creation turns on him. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Monster Men opens with a man dissolving a body in nitric acid to hide a crime. Professor Maxon seeks to restore his daughter's lost lover by artificial means.

Number 13, the latest creation, gains a soul and a name through love and suffering. Treachery, a bull whip, and buried treasure drive the middle chapters. Virginia Maxon must judge man against monster. The novel blends horror, romance, and early science fiction. Burroughs asks whether a made man can claim a soul, a question later science fiction kept asking.
a-little-pilgrim-stories-of-the-seen-and:
A Little Pilgrim, published in 1888 by Margaret Oliphant, gathers stories of the seen and the unseen. Oliphant frames the collection with a remarkable opening: a woman describes what it felt like to come to the very point of death after a long illness, and to return. There was no pain in it, she says, only a sense of sinking down through everything that should have held her.

From that threshold, the stories follow a little pilgrim into the world beyond death. Oliphant imagines the unseen country gently, as a place of rest, learning, and reunion rather than terror. The collection became one of her best-loved works, offering Victorian readers a tender vision of what might wait after dying.
a-miscellany-of-men:
G. K. Chesterton sorts his essays by types of men, as his contents page shows. Here are the suffragist, the poet and the cheese, and the man who thinks backwards. Here too are the mad official, the free man, the fool, and the miser. Each essay takes one figure and turns him over in Chesterton's hands until he looks new.

Chesterton writes about voters, priests, journalists, and Scotsmen with jokes that carry arguments about democracy, faith, and common sense. His method is paradox: defend the ordinary man against the experts, and find wisdom in old customs. The pieces first appeared as journalism, and they keep a newspaper's pace and sparkle.
a-siren:
Thomas Adolphus Trollope's A Siren unfolds in six books around Ravenna at Carnival. Book one begins on Ash Wednesday morning, after the last night of Carnival. The diva has vanished, and the city wakes to scandal. Books two to four go back four months to tell how the trouble began.

Paolina Foscarelli, the siren singer, arrives with an impresario's report and a great love to be taught. The Marchese Lamberto di Castelmare, his uncle, a cardinal, and a contessa circle her voice. Book five, Who Did the Deed?, turns the novel into a murder inquiry, with a post-mortem and a prison visit. The friar's testimony and the trial close the case. Thomas Adolphus, Anthony's elder brother, lived in Italy and wrote its modern life. His Ravenna of priests, attorneys, and opera is drawn from residence, not tourism.
advice-to-a-mother-on-the-management-of-:
Pye Henry Chavasse, a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, addresses mothers directly. His preface boasts of a thirteenth edition. The twelfth, of twenty thousand copies, had sold out in under three years. Translations into French, German, Polish, and Tamil followed. The contents divide the child's life into three parts: infancy, childhood, and boyhood and girlhood.

Each part covers washing, clothing, diet, exercise, sleep, and the nursery, then dentition, vaccination, ailments, and the treatment on the moment of pressing illnesses and accidents. Chavasse writes in a question-and-answer, conversational manner meant to calm a young mother at midnight. The manual was the child-care authority of its age, and it now reads as a full record of Victorian nursery practice.
aladdin-o-brien:
Gouverneur Morris opens Aladdin O'Brien with Poe's Annabel Lee and a forbidden river. Aladdin entices Margaret from Sunday-school to a skiff he barely knows how to row. He whistles through his front teeth and blows grapevine smoke through his nose. To be with him, the narrator says, was a delicious lesson in corruption.

The river nearly drowns them both, and Margaret's scarf becomes the book's token. Aladdin grows into a charming, reckless young man of politics and newspapers. Washington draws the grown pair into its intrigues, where his luck and nerve keep rescuing him. Morris writes a picaresque of American charm: a boy with a lamp-like gift for escaping scrapes. Margaret's steady love measures the man against the child. The novel's lightness is deliberate, a fairy tale of the republic's capital.
arnim-die-majoratsherren:
Property passed rigidly from heir to heir becomes a curse in Arnim's Die Majoratsherren, given here in German. The Lords of the Entailed Estate turns a dry legal institution, the entail, into the engine of a dark family drama. Inheritance and family pride grind the characters between them like millstones.

Arnim blends realism with the uncanny in his characteristic way, letting old houses and older papers gather menace. Portraits, wills, and decaying rooms carry the family's buried guilt. The novella asks what wealth does to love when law forbids it to move freely. German Romanticism rarely aimed its strangeness at so concrete a target. The result reads like a ghost story with a lawyer in it.
arnim-isabella-von-agypten:
Gypsy wanderers and settled townsfolk collide in Achim von Arnim's novella Isabella von Aegypten, presented in German. Isabella, a young gypsy leader, crosses into a richly imagined past of emperors and camps. Love strains against the boundary between her people and the settled world that fears them.

Arnim helped collect the folk songs of Des Knaben Wunderhorn, and that folk learning saturates his fiction. Antiquarian detail and Romantic invention braid together here into something strange and beautiful. The novella asks who belongs and who must wander, questions its century pressed hard. Its heroine carries both pride and sorrow in equal measure. Few German tales of the period feel so lush and so sad at once.
b09-hutten-obscure-men:
Epistolae Obscurorum Virorum, Letters of Obscure Men, appeared in Latin in 1515 as a joke with teeth. Crotus Rubeanus began the mock letters, and Ulrich von Hutten wrote much of the crushing second part of 1517. The letters pretend to come from dim scholastic monks writing to a master at Cologne.

In bad Latin and worse logic, the fake monks expose their own folly on every page. The satire struck the Cologne scholars who had hounded the humanist Reuchlin and his Hebrew studies. Learned Europe laughed, and the old school of theology never shook off the scorn. The work stands as the great humanist satire on the eve of the Reformation.
bashful-fifteen: Bashful Fifteen, by L. T. Meade. The shy girl's tale. This book preserves that story. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
bimbi-stories-for-children:
Bimbi, stories for children by Ouida, the pen name of Louise de la Ramee, gathers five tales written with a painter's eye for place. The longest and best known, The Nurnberg Stove, opens in Hall, a little town in Austria's Upper Inn valley. Ouida describes its green meadows, glacier fed river, latticed shop panes, and grand Gothic church before she ever introduces August, the boy who knows no other world.

August's treasure is a great porcelain stove, and the tale follows his fight to keep it when hard times press his family. Around it the collection sets The Ambitious Rose Tree, Lampblack, The Child of Urbino, and Findelkind, stories of plants, artists, and lost children across Italy and Germany. Ouida wrote for adults chiefly, but her children's tales keep her signature style: rich scenery, tender feeling, and beauty treated as a serious matter.
biographies-of-working-men:
Grant Allen's Biographies of Working Men, published in 1884, tells seven lives of men who rose from labour. Thomas Telford, the stonemason who became a great engineer, opens the volume. Allen begins with Telford's birth in a shepherd's cottage in Eskdale in 1757. His widowed mother raised him on her own ten fingers.

George Stephenson the engine-man and John Gibson the sculptor follow. William Herschel, once a bandsman, reached the stars as an astronomer. Jean François Millet the painter and James Garfield the canal boy turned president carry the theme abroad. Thomas Edward, a shoemaker naturalist, closes the set. Allen drew on earlier lives by Samuel Smiles and others. The book preaches energy and perseverance to working readers, Victorian self-help at its most earnest.
bonnie-prince-charlie-a-tale-of-fontenoy:
G. A. Henty's Bonnie Prince Charlie tells the Jacobite rising through the battles of Fontenoy and Culloden. The tale opens on a dull September evening in 1728, when Bailie Anderson's household sits down to supper above the shop, apprentices eyeing the food while grace drags on.

A knock at the door breaks the meal, and the old servant must peer through the grille before opening, since these are not times to admit a stranger lightly. From that domestic opening Henty builds toward the Young Pretender's cause, Highland campaigns and the disaster of Culloden. Young readers of historical adventure will find Henty's usual blend of domestic detail and battlefield action.
books-and-bookmen:
Andrew Lang's Books and Bookmen, printed by Longmans in 1887, opens with a verse dedication asking whether ladies can care for gossip of texts and bindings old. Chapters follow on Elzevir editions, curiosities of parish registers, the Rowfant library, Japanese bogie-books, and ghosts in the library. Literary forgeries and bibliomania in France get long treatments.

Lang retells how the Shakespeare Society was taken in by young William Henry Ireland's sham documents, with Boswell kneeling to kiss the relics. A bookman's purgatory and lady book-lovers round out the miscellany. The volume defined the amiable amateur tradition in English book collecting: learned, funny, and more interested in readers than in prices.
brood-of-the-witch-queen: Brood of the Witch-Queen, Sax Rohmer's occult thriller. The witch's brood. This book preserves that horror. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
business-hints-for-men-and-women:
Business Hints for Men and Women, by A R Calhoun, is a practical manual for farmers and small property holders who must handle their own paperwork. Calhoun opens with common sense farming. Wealth, land, labor, and money come first. The farmer is a producer and seller. He needs business methods as much as a plow. From the farm he moves to the desk.

Whole chapters teach documents a countryman actually signs. Deeds and abstracts of title come first, then forms of deeds and mortgages, payments, assignments, and the equity of redemption, the borrower's right to recover his land. Wills get a chapter of kinds, limits, and executive duties. Letter writing closes the early course, with forms for business letters and letters of introduction. The book belongs to the era when a farm was a firm, and its owner was expected to be his own lawyer at the kitchen table.
c-f-meyer-das-leiden-eines-knaben:
A gentle boy suffers under the cruelty of the adult world in C. F. Meyer's Das Leiden eines Knaben, given here in German. The Sufferings of a Boy tells its sad story with restraint and deep sympathy. School discipline, a harsh father figure, and a child's helplessness close around the young hero.

Meyer, himself a late bloomer who knew suffering from inside, writes with unforgettable tenderness. Nothing is exaggerated, which makes the boy's fate harder to bear. The novella ranks among literature's most heartbreaking portraits of childhood wronged. Its quiet protest against needless severity has not lost force. Readers often finish it in one sitting and sit silent afterward.
canada-for-gentlemen:
James Seton Cockburn's Canada for Gentlemen prints the letters of a young emigrant, sent home to his family circle and published by his father. The elder Cockburn explains that friends were so eager to read the manuscript letters that printing them saved the originals from wearing out.

The letters describe the real difficulties of young emigrants, a subject the emigration agencies said little about, and their lessons are often more valuable than tales of uniform success. Fictitious names replace those of friends, and the father hopes the price of the book may even buy the writer his winter furs. Readers interested in emigration, or in Canada as newcomers actually found it, will find these letters frank and useful.
carmen:
Prosper Mérimée told Carmen as a tale inside a tale, in Lady Mary Loyd's translation. His narrator, an archaeologist hunting a Roman battlefield in Andalusia in 1830, falls in with the smuggler Don José and hears his confession. José, a Basque soldier, let a gypsy cigarette girl named Carmen escape arrest, joined her smugglers, and slid from love into jealous murder among the mountains.

Mérimée keeps the telling dry and swift, letting Carmen's freedom and José's obsession collide without excuse or sermon. The story later fed Bizet's opera, which softened what Mérimée left hard. Read here in its original form, Carmen is a cool, fatal little masterpiece about a woman who would rather die than be owned.
castren-ethnologische-vorlesungen:
Castrén's Ethnological Lectures on the Altaic Peoples appeared in German in 1857. The lectures give the great Finn's summing of his life's work. Turks, Mongols, and Tungus peoples stand in one wide frame.

Castrén compares their tongues, faiths, and ways from his own travel notes. He died young after reshaping the whole field he founded here. The talks became a founding text of Ural-Altaic studies for Europe. Students across the north took their first map of the field from him. His calm, vast scheme still earns respect from scholars across the north today. The lectures turn hard travel into ordered, lasting knowledge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aachen:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Aachen describes the city known in French as Aix-la-Chapelle and in Latin as Aquae Grani. Aachen lies in a Prussian valley among wooded heights, on the Wurm stream, and owes its origin to health-giving springs already known to the Romans.

Charlemagne chose Aachen as his favourite residence, adorning it with an imperial palace and chapel where he wished to be buried. Relics gathered by Charlemagne and Otto the Third drew medieval shrine pilgrimages from across Europe, and thirty-seven German emperors were crowned there between 813 and 1531. Later religious strife, bans of the empire and Protestant risings troubled the city, yet its chapel and pilgrimage tradition endured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Ouen describes a Benedictine house at Rouen reaching to Merovingian times. Its foundation is credited variously to Clothair the First and to St. Clothilda, without sufficient evidence to settle the question.

First dedicated to St. Peter, the house took St. Ouen's name after the Archbishop of Rouen, dead in 678, was buried there. Its recorded history from 1000 holds nothing exceptional, and in 1660 it joined the Congregation of St. Maur, numbering twenty-four at its suppression in 1794. The abbey's chief interest lies in its glorious church, larger and lovelier than Rouen Cathedral, begun in 1318 by Abbot Jean Roussel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-wald:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Waldsassen, meaning settlement in the woods, describes a famed Cistercian house on the Wondreb in the Upper Palatinate, near Bohemia's border. Gerwich von Wolmundstein, a Benedictine monk of Sigeberg, built it between 1128 and 1132 with his former abbot Kuno's leave.

The first monks came from Volkenrod in Thuringia, of Morimond's line, and the first abbot was elected in 1133. Waldsassen soon ranked among the most famed and strong houses of the age, founding Sedlitz and Ossegg in Bohemia and Walderbach near Regensburg. Several of its thirty-seven abbots before the Reformation were famed for holiness and learning, though wars, famines, taxes and attacks later brought swings of good times and decay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aberdeen:
Aberdeen is a Scottish see founded in 1063 at Mortlach by Blessed Beyn. Its first firm record is a bull of Adrian IV from 1157, confirming its churches and lands to Bishop Edward. The granite cathedral went up in 1272-1277. Bishop Thomas Spence's Franciscan house dates to 1480, and Bishop Elphinstone's King's College at Old Aberdeen to 1505. The see moved to Old Aberdeen about 1125 and stayed there until 1577, served by twenty-nine bishops.

From 1653 prefects-apostolic governed Scotland's Catholics, followed by vicars-apostolic. In 1878 Leo XIII restored the Scottish hierarchy, and John MacDonald became first bishop of the restored see. Aberdeen became one of four suffragan sees under St. Andrews and Edinburgh. The entry also notes Fort Augustus, raised to an abbey directly subject to Rome in 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-contzen:
Adam Contzen was an economist and exegete born in 1573, or 1575 by Sommervogel, at Montjoie in Julich. He died at Munich on 19 June 1635. He joined the Jesuits at Trier in 1595 and taught philosophy at Wurzburg in 1606. He moved to Mainz in 1610, holding Holy Scripture's chair for over ten years. He helped organize the University of Molsheim in Alsace, serving as chancellor in 1622 and 1623.

Contzen was a learned, versatile writer on controversy, political economy, and scripture. He defended Bellarmine against Pareus of Heidelberg. When Pareus sought to unite Calvinists and Lutherans against Catholics, Contzen showed the project's impracticality in De Pace Germaniae of 1616. In 1623 he published commentaries on the Gospels and Pauline epistles, plus a political novel on an Abyssinian king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-breme:
Adam of Bremen was an eleventh-century German historian and geographer, whose birth and death dates are unknown. His Gesta Hammaburgensis Ecclesiae Pontificum covers the Hamburg see and northern Christian missions from 788 to 1072. Northern regions before the thirteenth century are known chiefly through it. In his preface he signs himself only by the initial A.

Helmold's Slavic Chronicle identifies A as Adam, author of the Hamburg church history. That he came from Saxony, more precisely Meissen, is mere conjecture from dialect traces in the work. He reached Bremen in 1068 at Archbishop Adalbert's invitation, was made cathedral canon and director of schools, and signed an official document on 11 June 1069. Soon after arriving he journeyed to King Svend Estridson of Denmark, famed for knowledge of northern history and geography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agen:
Agen, ancient Aginnum, is a French diocese comprising the Lot and Garonne department. It has been successively suffragan to Bordeaux under the old regime, to Toulouse from 1802 to 1822, and to Bordeaux since 1822. Legends no older than the ninth century about the hermit St. Caprasius, martyred alongside St. Fides under Dacianus, and the story of Vincentius, written about 520, give no foundation for traditions making these saints Agen's early bishops.

History's first known bishop, St. Phoebadius, was St. Hilary's friend and published a treatise against the Arians in 357 and figured at the Council of Rimini in 359. Later bishops include Wilhelmus II, sent by Urban IV to St. Louis in 1262, Bertrand de Goth, uncle of Clement V, Cardinal Jean de Lorraine, the preacher Jules Mascaron, and de Bonnac, first to refuse the constitutional oath in 1792. The church of St. Caprasius, a fine Romance building, is now the cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-aac:
Albert of Aachen, also called Albertus Aquensis, was a chronicler of the First Crusade, now usually thought to have been a canon of Aachen. His Chronicle of Jerusalem on the Holy War, in twelve books covering 1095 to 1121, survives in early printed collections of crusade histories. Whether he belonged instead to the church of Aix-en-Provence remains doubtful, the entry notes, following Wattenbach.

The entry judges his narrative harshly on method: it has little order, less critical skill, inexact chronology, and often mangled place names. Yet it values the work as the writing of a deeply religious man with a poet's heart. He saw Christian knighthood as the salvation of Christendom. In that light, it says, the severe criticism of von Sybel loses much of its point.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-nam:
Seven men named Alexander appear in Scripture. Alexander the Great, King of Macedon from 336 to 323 B.C., is mentioned in 1 Maccabees and is thought to figure in Daniel's visions. Alexander Balas, eleventh King of Syria from 150 to 145 B.C., won his throne with promises to Jonathan, followed a pro-Jewish policy, and was beaten by his father-in-law Ptolemy Philometor. Alexander, son of Simon of Cyrene, is named by St. Mark as a son of the man who carried the cross after Jesus.

Another Alexander sat on Peter and John's trial court, and some identify him with Alexander Lysimachus, brother of Philo. A further Alexander, Jew or Jewish Christian, tried to defend St. Paul, and some identify him with Simon's son. The last two are an Ephesian Christian who fell away with Hymenaeus and a coppersmith who did St. Paul evil. Some take them to be the same man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonse-magn:
Alphonse Magnien, clergy educator, was born at Bleymard in 1837 and died in 1902. A classics student at Chirac and philosophy and theology student at Orléans, he showed brilliant talents and character. He joined Orléans on Dupanloup's appeal. In the seminary a Sulpician vocation grew in him, postponed by the bishop. For two years after ordination he taught at La Chapelle St-Mesmin. He then taught sciences at Nantes and theology and Scripture at Rodez.

In fall 1869 he began Baltimore work, known to American priests. At St. Mary's he taught philosophy, later Scripture and dogma. He grasped a question's vital part instinctively, resting only on truth. After Dubreul's death in 1878, Magnien became superior. For a quarter century he shaped American clergy formation. Upright, frank, manly, a true priest devoted to the Church, he was most at home on the rostrum. Speaking almost daily on spiritual topics, he never tired hearers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-screen:
The altar screen is embroidered needlework, cloth of gold, or tapestry, as wide as the altar and sometimes extending along its sides. It hangs above a high altar attached to the wall or within three feet of it. It bears images of Our Lord, the Blessed Virgin, or saints, unless such images are already painted on the wall.

A permanent screen has a base as long as table and steps, a panel framing picture, bas-relief, or statue, and a cornice of frieze and pediment topped by a cross. Metal served in the eleventh century, stone in the thirteenth, wood from the fourteenth. Folding doors sometimes covered the picture except on grand festivals. Its nave-facing side is the retable, its reverse the counter-retable. Enriched with niches, statues, and buttresses, it becomes a reredos, sometimes spanning the church's breadth nearly to the ceiling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amen:
Amen is one of few Hebrew words imported unchanged into the Church's liturgy, for its exceptionally sacred example, as Augustine put it. Trent's Catechism notes how frequent it was in Our Saviour's mouth, Matthew attributing it to him twenty-eight times and John twenty-six in doubled form. It derives from Hebrew aman, to strengthen or confirm.

In Scripture it works almost always as an adverb, adopting another's words as one's own, as Jeremiah answering Hananias in chapter 28, verse 6. Synagogue use as the people's answer to aloud prayer passed to Apostolic-age Christians. A third use closes discourses or chapters with a doxology ending in Amen, now a mere formula. Two special cases earn separate treatment: the people's Amen closing the great Prayer of Consecration, and the Amen after Communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold-jansse:
Arnold Janssen, founder and first head of the Society of the Divine Word, was born at Goch in the Rhine Province on 5 November 1837. He died at Steyl in Holland on 15 January 1909. From a very young age he showed an inclination for priesthood. After classical studies at Gaesdonck college, philosophy at Münster academy, and theology at Bonn and Münster, he was ordained on 15 August 1861.

He spent years in pastoral work and teaching Christian doctrine, becoming chaplain and head at the Ursuline convent of Kempen in 1873. As diocesan head of the Apostleship of Prayer he laboured to spread that association, and in that role felt called to found a missionary base for Germany. The result was Steyl's Mission House of St. Michael, opened 8 September 1875, from which the Society of the Divine Word grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baden:
Baden was a Grand Duchy in the southwest of the German Empire, bounded by Switzerland, Alsace, and Bavaria. It covered 5,821 square miles, and its 1905 census counted 2,010,728 people. Catholics numbered 1,198,511, Evangelicals 762,826, and Jews 25,893, among other faiths. At the Christian era its land formed the tithe lands, guarded by a wall against German tribes.

After Emperor Probus died in 282, the Alemanni seized the southern tithe lands. Frankish victories in 496 and 536 made them masters of the region. Pepin the Short ended tribal dukedoms in 748 and set Frankish imperial order in place. Frankish power brought Christianity: Columbanus and Gall worked the south about 610, Pirminius followed a century later. Trudpert labored in the Breisgau, Kilian in the northeast, and Mainz evangelized the Rhine valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-ernst-v:
Baron Ernst von Feuchtersleben was an Austrian poet, philosopher, and physician, born at Vienna in 1806, who died in 1849. After the Theresian Academy he studied medicine from 1825 and took his doctorate in 1833. In 1844 he began free lectures on psychiatry at Vienna, became faculty dean in 1845, and vice-director of medico-chirurgical studies in 1847. In July 1848 he became under-secretary for public instruction, but resigned, discouraged by reform's difficulties.

His Zur Diätetik der Seele of 1838 brought him great popularity and ran to a forty-sixth edition by 1896. His 1845 textbook of medical psychology appeared in English as Principles of Medical Psychology in 1847. As a poet he is best known for the song Es ist bestimmt in Gottes Rat, set to music by Mendelssohn. His complete non-medical works were edited by Friedrich Hebbel in seven volumes from 1851 to 1853.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-guillau:
Baron Guillaume Dupuytren was a French anatomist and surgeon, born at Pierre-Buffière in 1777, who died at Paris in 1835. His poor parents sent him to the Collège de la Marche on charity. By competitive examination he became anatomy's prosecutor at Paris's new medical school at eighteen. In 1803 he became assistant surgeon at the Hôtel-Dieu, and by 1815 its head surgeon and professor of clinical surgery.

Indefatigable, he built one of the largest surgical practices of all time and amassed a great fortune. He battled a consumptive tendency all his life, and it finally carried him off. His will endowed the anatomy chair at the medical school and founded a home for physicians in distress. The palm contraction crippling the fingers still bears his name, and his chief writings treat the artificial anus and gunshot wounds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-von-mun:
Baron von Münch-Bellinghausen, writing as Friedrich Halm, was an Austrian dramatist born at Cracow in 1806, who died at Vienna in 1871. Schooled at Melk and Vienna in philosophy and law, he began an official career in 1826. His teacher Enk von der Burg urged his Griseldis on the Hofburg theatre, and its 1835 success fixed his reputation. He rose to Government councillor in 1840 and keeper of the Court Library in 1844, a post Grillparzer had sought in vain.

His best-known plays are Griseldis, The Son of the Wilderness (1842), and The Gladiator of Ravenna (1857). Griseldis tests a faithful wife's loyalty to triumph, while Son of the Wilderness sets womanly love against barbarian strength. He also wrote lyrics, stories, and the narrative poem Charfreitag, and superintended the court theatres from 1867 to 1870. His complete works appeared at Vienna in eight volumes, with four more posthumously.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-van-:
Benedict van Haeften, a Benedictine writer and provost of Afflighem, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Utrecht in 1588, he died at Spa in 1648 while seeking his health. After study at Louvain, he entered Afflighem in 1609, took vows in 1611, and was ordained priest in 1613.

He became prior in 1616 and provost, or head, of the monastery in 1618, guiding it through a dispute over joining a stricter congregation. Under his prudent rule the house flourished in spirit and in goods. His chief book, a twelve-volume study of the Rule of St. Benedict, appeared at Antwerp in 1644, with six shorter devotional works beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bohemian-bret:
The Bohemian Brethren, also called Moravian Brethren or Unitas Fratrum, put lived faith before creeds and took Scripture as their only rule of faith. Founded in Bohemia in 1457 and renewed by Count Zinzendorf in 1722, the body still lived when the entry was written. Personal faith in the crucified Saviour grounds its fellowship, while debate over doctrines like the Trinity is shunned.

Its history runs from Wyclif through Hus, whose burning at Constance in 1415 outraged Bohemia. The entry follows the old Unitas Fratrum to 1722, then the renewed brotherhood under Zinzendorf. Later sections cover the Brethren in England, the Moravian Church in America, and the body's present condition, with baptism and the Lord's Supper as its only sacraments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bremen:
Bremen, once an archdiocese on the lower Weser and Elbe, began with Saint Willehad, consecrated bishop in 787 after Charlemagne's Saxon conquest. He chose Bremen, first named in 782, and built a cathedral dedicated in 789. The diocese itself rose only under his successor Willerich, and after Leuderich's death in 845, Mainz joined Bremen to Hamburg's archdiocese under Saint Anschar.

Hamburg's Viking ruin in 845 pushed the see toward Bremen, though the title moved formally only in 1223. Nicholas I confirmed the union in 864 against Cologne's protests, and Formosus freed Bremen from Cologne in 892. Rembert and Adalgar, Benedictines from Corvey, advanced the northern missions, Hungarians burned city and diocese under Hoger, and Unni died at Birka in 936 on a Scandinavian mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brixen:
Brixen, a prince-bishopric of Austria suffragan to Salzburg, covers most of northern Tyrol and all Vorarlberg across 6,705 square miles with over 440,000 people. It continues the see of Saben, where Christianity reached a Roman customs post by the third century and Ingenuin stands as first proven bishop about 580. Bajuvari and Lombards took the faith early, though Puster Valley Slavs held paganism until the eighth century.

Bishop Rihpert or Albuin moved the seat to Brixen in the late tenth century, Hartwig raised it to a city, and emperors showered it with land. Frederick I made its bishop a prince of the empire in 1179, which helps explain why Brixen's bishops backed emperors against popes, notably at the 1080 pseudo-synod deposing Gregory VII. Later bishops fiefed away much land to Tyrol's counts, shrinking their own temporal power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cap-haitien:
Cap-Haïtien is a Haitian diocese erected by Pius IX in October 1861 within the province of Port-au-Prince. It covers the northern department of the island republic. In 1906 it counted some 650,000 Catholics, more than a quarter of Haiti's people. The land forms the western third of Santo Domingo, the second largest of the Greater Antilles.

Its history runs from Columbus's second voyage in 1493, when Dominicans came to the island. Jesuit and Franciscan parish work followed, with a large Jesuit hospital. Later bishops built schools for boys and girls and a diocesan seminary. The entry closes with the diocese's religious and educational state, including Masonic lodges that once drew members when clergy were scarce. They now gather only a few times a year for festivals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catechumen:
A catechumen was a person in the early Church who had not yet been baptized but was preparing for initiation. The word comes from the Greek verb for being instructed, and it appears in Galatians, Corinthians, Luke, and Acts. Since accepting Christianity meant believing a body of doctrine and keeping the divine law, converts needed some teaching first, simple and short in apostolic times.

As churches became organized, the preparation grew longer and more formal. The article explains that the danger of apostasy, or even betrayal during persecution, led to special precautions around admission. It traces how a short instruction for Jews and pagans developed into a regulated period of probation before the sacred mysteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-le-go:
A life of Charles Le Gobien, the French Jesuit who founded the celebrated Lettres édifiantes et curieuses, a vast collection of missionary letters. Born at St-Malo in 1671, he entered the Society of Jesus. As procurator of the French mission to China, he worked to stir educated readers to support the spread of Christianity in East Asia. His own writings took up the progress of religion in China and the fierce dispute over Chinese rites, the ceremonies honouring Confucius and the dead.

In 1702 he issued letters from Jesuit missionaries in China and the East Indies, the seed of a collection that grew to thirty-six volumes by 1776, with later reissues and abridgements. It remains a key source for the history of Catholic missions, preserving first-hand reports from distant stations. Le Gobien also wrote a history of the newly converted Mariana Islands before his early death in Paris in 1708.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-plowd:
An entry on the Tudor lawyer Edmund Plowden, whose legal writings and courtroom wit made him famous. Humphrey Plowden's son, of Plowden Hall, Shropshire, he was educated at Cambridge without taking a degree. Called to the Middle Temple in 1538, he was praised by Camden as the greatest lawyer of his age. He also qualified as a surgeon and physician in 1552.

Under Mary he sat in Parliament and served on the Council of the Marches of Wales. His Catholic faith blocked promotion under Elizabeth, who is said to have offered him the lord chancellorship if he joined the Anglican Church. Defending a man charged with hearing Mass, he won an acquittal by showing the service had been staged by a lay informer, crying, in effect, no priest, no Mass. The episode gave rise to the proverb, the case is altered, quoth Plowden. His Commentaries appeared in 1571.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-churching-of-:
An entry on the churching of women, the Church's blessing of mothers recovered from childbirth. Only a Catholic woman who bore a child in lawful wedlock may receive it. It is a pious custom from the early ages, not a precept. As soon as she can leave home, the mother presents herself in church to thank God for a happy delivery and to gain grace for raising her child Christianly.

The prayers bless the mother alone, so the child need not come, though many places dedicate the child to God as well. The blessing is given even if the child was stillborn or died unbaptised. Churching is not strictly parochial, yet a parish priest asked to give it must do so. It must be given where Mass is celebrated, since the rite is a pilgrimage of thanksgiving to the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-frasse:
Claude Frassen, a Scotist theologian of the Friars Minor, was born near Peronne in 1620 and died at Paris on 26 February 1711. He entered the Franciscans at Peronne at seventeen, finished his studies at Paris, and stayed as professor of philosophy and theology for thirty years. In 1662 he became a Sorbonne doctor and definitor general, elected in 1682, attending general chapters at Toledo and Rome. Louis the Fourteenth held him in high esteem.

Frassen died at ninety-one, after seventy-four years in religion. His best-known work, Scotus Academicus, ranks among the most important presentations of Duns Scotus's theology. Few interpreters of Scotus match his blend of simple style, clear method, and Scotistic subtlety, with quotations from the Fathers and statements of controverted questions. Its first volume lists heresies from Christian beginnings to the 1400s. The Rome edition of 1900 to 1902 runs to twelve volumes from his notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-of-:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry traces children's Communion through ancient practice and present discipline. Early Christians often gave infants Communion right after baptism. Saint Cyprian notes the practice. In the East it ran nearly universal and lingers in places still. In the West it stayed narrower, kept to baptism and dangerous illness. It may have sprung from a mistaken idea that the Eucharist was absolutely needed for salvation, drawn from John chapter six.

Present law was settled by the Fourth Lateran Council and later confirmed. A keener religious sense is asked for Communion than for confession. Pastors bear the weighty duty of preparing children for First Communion. Morrisroe lists the norms: pascal time, the parish church as a rule, lasting impression on the child, and a solemn Mass with boys and girls attired and seated apart. A short address may precede the distribution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-von-bo:
Barnabas Dieringer's entry follows Conrad von Bolanden, pen name of Joseph Bischoff, German novelist born at Niedergeilbach in 1828, son of a rich merchant. He attended Blieskastel's Latin school and Speyer's seminary, then Munich University for theology in 1849. Ordained in 1852, he served as cathedral assistant pastor. Two years later he became pastor at Kirchheim Bolanden, source of his pen name, then at Börrstadt and Berghausen.

During these years he wrote A Wedding Trip, Queen Bertha, Historical Tales of Frederick II, and Gustav Adolf. In 1870 he resigned his parish for literary work alone, living in retirement at Speyer. Later novels include Canossa, Trowel or Cross, Night of Saint Bartholomew, Savonarola, Crusades, Wambold, Charlemagne, and Otto the Great. Written for the people, brilliant and simple, they defend the Catholic standpoint with original sources. Day's questions draw severe, unjust criticism, yet the works found wide readers and translations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelis-enge:
George Williamson's entry treats Cornelis Engelbrechtsen, also Engelberts and Engelbrecht, now usually Engelbrechtsz. The Dutch painter, born at Leyden in 1468 and died there in 1533, may be Cornelis de Hollandere, of Antwerp's Guild of Saint Luke in 1492. He is said to have been Holland's first oil painter, and a profound student of Jan Van Eyck.

His principal paintings were executed in Leyden. The city still holds his large Crucifixion, its wings showing the Sacrifice of Abraham and the Brazen Serpent, and a Pietà with six scenes from Christ's life. A Madonna and Child hangs in London's National Gallery, a Crucifixion in Munich, and two double pictures at Antwerp. Most of his religious works perished in Holland's sixteenth-century iconoclastic movement. His sons were Cornelis, called Kunst, 1493 to 1544, and Luke, called Kok. Luke came to England under Henry VIII, and a signed picture of his sits at Penshurst.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-ammen:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Ammen, an American naval officer and author born in Ohio in 1820 and dead at Washington in 1898. Appointed midshipman in 1834, he studied briefly at West Point under his brother Jacob, later a Union general, and rose to lieutenant in 1849 and rear admiral in 1877. In the Civil War he served on blockade duty with Admiral Dupont's fleet.

Ashore, he led the Bureau of Yards and Docks and then the Bureau of Navigation until retirement in 1878. He designed the ram Katahdin and the Ammen balsa life raft. He championed a Nicaraguan canal, serving on the 1872 commission that backed that route and as delegate to the 1879 Paris congress. In retirement he farmed at Ammendale, where his generosity built Saint Joseph's church, and wrote naval memoirs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dresden:
Dresden, capital of the Kingdom of Saxony and home of its royal family, lies on both banks of the Elbe, crossed there by five bridges and ringed by pleasant heights. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts, with suburbs, over five hundred thousand people in December 1905. Most were Evangelical Lutherans, with some forty-four thousand Catholics, three thousand Jews, and a small Reformed body.

Dresden housed the vicar apostolic for Saxony, the Catholic consistory, and the vicarial court. In 1907 it counted twenty-four clergy, six Catholic parish churches, a garrison church shared with Protestants, and schools and charities. The entry closes with Dresden histories and journals for readers who want the city's Catholic story in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-plowde:
Edmund Plowden was an English Jesuit of the age of suppression and restoration, born in 1743 and dead in France in 1821. Schooled at Saint Omer, he joined the Society in 1759 and was ordained at Rome in 1770. When the Society was suppressed in 1773 he was minister of the English College at Bruges, and the local government kept him locked up for months after the college closed.

Freed, he taught at Liege, served as chaplain at Lulworth, and preached at the consecration of Bishop Carroll in 1790. He helped run Stonyhurst College from its start in 1794, became the first master of novices when the Society returned in England, and was made provincial in 1817. Dying on the road home from Rome, he was buried with full military honours by mistake, since townsfolk took him for an army general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-arden:
Edward Arden was a Warwickshire Catholic gentleman put to death in 1583, in a case the entry calls a plain miscarriage of justice. Head of a family prominent in the county for six centuries, he had been high sheriff in 1575. His father was a second cousin of Mary Arden, the mother of Shakespeare. Arden kept a priest, Father Hugh Hall, at Park Hall disguised as a gardener.

His son-in-law John Somerville, angered by the wrongs of Mary Queen of Scots, spoke threats against Queen Elizabeth. Seized and racked, Somerville named Arden in a plot to kill the queen. Tried at Guildhall in London on 16 December 1583, Arden was convicted largely on Hall's word and hanged at Smithfield two weeks later, still protesting that his only crime was his faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-haward:
Edward Hawarden, also spelled Harden, was an English theologian and controversialist born in Lancashire in 1662 and dead in London in 1735. His family kept private chapels through persecution and often appears on recusant rolls. After a brilliant course at Douai he taught classics and philosophy there, was ordained in 1686, and took the chair of divinity.

In 1688 he spent two months teaching divinity at Magdalen College, Oxford, which James II meant to make a Catholic seat of learning, but the revolution sent him back to Douai. Charges that he spread Jansenism were cleared by Rome. From 1707 he worked on missions at Gilligate and Aldcliffe, then in London as a writer of controversy, winning Oxford's thanks for defending the Trinity against Samuel Clarke in 1719.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-patric:
Edward Patrick Allen was the fifth Bishop of Mobile, Alabama, born at Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1853. He took his college course at Mount Saint Mary's in Emmitsburg, Maryland, graduating in 1878, and stayed on there for theology. Ordained priest in December 1881, he taught at Mount Saint Mary's, then served as assistant at the Boston cathedral and at Framingham.

In 1884 he returned to Mount Saint Mary's as its president, a post he held until he was named Bishop of Mobile. He was consecrated at Baltimore in May 1897, and Georgetown University had given him a doctorate in divinity in 1889. The entry is a short record of steady academic and pastoral service rising, step by step, to the head of a southern diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-father-damien:
Father Damien was a Belgian missionary priest who served the lepers of Molokai. Born in 1840, he joined the Fathers of the Sacred Heart at Louvain. Sent to Hawaii in 1864, he built chapels with his own hands. In 1873 he volunteered as resident priest of the Molokai leper settlement.

Six hundred lepers lived there when he arrived, with almost no medical care. Damien dressed ulcers, raised cottages, dug graves, and made coffins. After twelve years he found the disease in himself, yet kept working. He died in 1889, his name later cleared of slander by Stevenson and others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frances-allen:
Frances Allen, born at Sunderland, Vermont, on 13 November 1784 and dead at Montreal on 10 September 1819, was the first New England-born woman to become a nun. Her father was Ethan Allen, the Revolutionary soldier and pioneer of Vermont, an atheist, and her stepfather also kept religion out of her mind as far as he could. Yet her keen, inquiring intellect drew her toward Catholic belief, and at twenty-one she asked to travel to Montreal, supposedly to learn French.

There she became a pupil of the Sisters of the Congregation of Notre Dame in 1807. A sister's simple request that she place flowers on an altar and adore the Real Presence began her deeper conversion. She entered religious life despite a background that made such a step seem least likely. The entry presents her short life as a striking case of conviction formed against family and circumstance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-plowd:
Francis Plowden, born in Shropshire on 8 June 1749 and dead at Paris on 4 January 1819, was a Catholic lawyer and historian of the penal-law age. Son of William Plowden of Plowden Hall, he was educated at St. Omer and entered the Jesuit novitiate at Watten in 1766. He was teaching at Bruges when the Society was suppressed, which freed him from his first vows since he was not yet in holy orders. He married Dorothea Phillips, entered the Middle Temple, and practised as a conveyancer, the only legal work then open to Catholics.

 Quarrels with the Lord Chancellor, improvidence, and extreme views ended his practice, and he turned to writing. His Historical Review of the State of Ireland, written for the government in 1803, condemned too outspokenly for their taste and drew sharp replies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-philip-:
Franz Philip Kaulen, born at Dusseldorf on 20 March 1827 and died at Bonn on 11 July 1907, was a German scriptural scholar who gave his life to the Bible. Schooled at Dusseldorf, he studied theology at Bonn from 1846 to 1849 and was ordained at Cologne on 3 September 1850. He served missions in Cologne diocese and became lecturer at Bonn's theological school in 1859. He took a doctorate at Wurzburg in 1862 for a commentary on Jonah and won the Old Testament chair at Bonn in 1863. He became extraordinary and ordinary professor of theology in 1880 and 1882.

 His works include a Manchu grammar of 1875, a study of the confusion of languages at Babel, and above all his editorship of Herder's great Church Lexicon. He contributed many articles to it. In its 1882 preface he set the programme his work followed: depth of learning with church correctness and clear, intelligible presentation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-xaver-f:
Franz Xaver Freiherr von Wulfen, born at Belgrade on 5 November 1728 and died at Klagenfurt on 17 March 1805, was an Austrian Jesuit botanist and pioneer explorer of the Eastern Alps. Son of Lieutenant Field-Marshal Christian Friedrich von Wulfen, he finished studies at Kaschau and joined the Jesuits in 1745. He lived as student and teacher, chiefly of mathematics and physics, at Vienna, Graz, Neusohl, Gorz, Laibach, and from 1764 Klagenfurt, remaining there after the Jesuits' suppression.

From his twenty-second year he gave himself with keen zeal to botany. His unusual talent, exact observation and description, and tireless research over fifty years make him a leading botanist of the post-Linnaean age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-ber:
Friedrich Maassen, a professor of law born at Wismar in 1823, became a leading historian of canon law. After studying at Jena, Berlin, Kiel, and Rostock, he practiced as an advocate and took his degree in 1851. A convert to the Catholic faith soon after, he left public office hopes behind and turned to teaching at Bonn. His 1853 book on the Roman primacy won him swift scholarly fame.

Count Thun called him to Pesth in 1855, and chairs at Innsbruck, Graz, and Vienna followed. His great history of canon law sources reached only one volume, published at Graz in 1870. His articles, his Pseudoisidor studies, and his edition of Merovingian councils for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica filled the gap. He also denounced the Prussian Kulturkampf in ringing prose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Hausen, one of the earliest German minnesingers, sang of love in forms borrowed from France and died on crusade. His name first appears in a Mainz document of 1171, and his dialect points to the middle Rhine, though several towns claim his birth. He served at Italian courts, met Frederick Barbarossa, and rode with the emperor's crusade of 1189.

Hausen fell with his horse at Philomelium in May 1190 while chasing the enemy, and the whole army mourned him. With Veldeke he brought the Romance strain into German love song, shaping verses on a French ten-syllable line with dactylic beat. His rhymes stay rough at times, and his songs prize wordplay and artifice over plain feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fuenfkirchen:
Fünfkirchen, now Pécs in Hungary, is a diocese whose roots reach an early Christian burial chamber of the fourth century. Named for its five churches, it became a bishopric under King Stephen I in 1009, with the Frankish Benedictine Bonipert as first bishop. His successor Maurus raised a cathedral on the old church of Saint Peter and stands as Hungary's first church writer.

The see's fortunes swung with history: its school rose to a university in 1367, then faded after the Turkish victory of 1526. Turks held the city from 1543 and turned the cathedral into a mosque until 1687. Later bishops held synods, founded a lyceum, and restored the cathedral. By the article's count the diocese held 178 parishes, German, Magyar, and mixed alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-allen:
George Allen, an educator born at Milton, Vermont, in 1808, taught ancient languages at two universities before becoming a Catholic. He graduated from the University of Vermont in 1827 and was admitted to the bar in 1831. Turning to theology, he served as rector of an Episcopal church at Saint Albans, Vermont, from 1834 to 1837.

In 1837 Allen became professor of ancient languages at Delaware College in Newark. In 1845 he took the same chair at Philadelphia's university, later as professor of Greek. He entered the Catholic Church in 1847, midway through his Philadelphia career. He died at Worcester, Massachusetts, in May 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerhard-of-zu:
Gerhard of Zutphen, a mystical writer born in 1367, stood among the first Brothers of the Common Life. Founded by Gerard Groote and Florentius Radewyns at Deventer, the community prized plain living and high thinking, and Gerhard surpassed it in absorption in sacred science and oblivion of earthly things. As librarian, his strong grasp of moral theology and canon law helped the brothers meet prejudice against their way of life.

His best-known works, Homo Quidam and Beatus Vir, are almost identical, preserved in de la Bigne's Patristic Library. Two treatises on prayer and Scripture reading in the mother tongue are also ascribed to him. Controversialists like Ullmann have used his zeal for vernacular Scripture to tie the Brothers to the German Reformers, but his own arguments, as quoted, give that claim almost no foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerlac-peters:
Gerlac Peterssen, a contemplative born at Deventer in 1377 or 1378, lived the Brethren of the Common Life's quiet craft. He gave his days to calligraphy, copying manuscripts, teaching, and prayer, keeping company with Rucksack, Radon, Kale, Gerard of Zutphen, the à Kempis brothers, and Vos of Hayden. When Radon founded Windesheim's monastery of regular canons in 1386, Gerlac followed and stayed until 1403 as a simple clerk, his only post that of sexton.

Called another Kempis, Gerlac left his brethren for his cell, saying somebody waited for him there. Critics have credited Kempis with Gerlac's words and theories, and the Imitation is said to reproduce his ascetic spirit. Thomas à Kempis even copied into his 1441 Imitation Gerlac's Soliloquies passage accepting hell forever for God's greater glory, an interpolation soon deleted. The two men's ascetic theories differ numerously and deeply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gnesen-posen:
Gnesen-Posen is an archdiocese in the Kingdom of Prussia, joining the dioceses of Gnesen and Posen, separate until 1821, under one archbishop, with the bishopric of Culm in its province. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces both sees from their tenth-century foundations.

Posen was founded in 968 under Duke Miecyslaw, baptized through his wife Dubravka, with Jordan as first bishop, suffragan to Magdeburg. Gnesen rose around the shrine of Saint Adalbert, martyred by the heathen Prussians. Otto III made it an archbishopric on his pilgrimage in 1000, creating Cracow, Breslau, and Kolberg as its suffragans. Since the twelfth century Posen has been undisputedly a suffragan of Gnesen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-hensc:
Godfrey Henschen, also called Henskens, was a Jesuit hagiographer born at Venray in Limburg on 21 June 1601, who died at Antwerp on 11 September 1681. Son of a cloth merchant, he studied at the Jesuit college of Bois-le-Duc and entered the novitiate at Mechlin in 1619. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the collaborator who gave the Acta Sanctorum its definitive form.

Ordained priest in 1634 and sent to Antwerp the next year, he joined Father Bollandus on the first volumes of the Acta Sanctorum. His commentary on the Acts of Saint Amand suggested the course to follow and shaped the scientific work. He collaborated on seventeen volumes, January through the first six of May. He journeyed with Papebroch through Italy, France, and Germany from 1660 to 1662, and served as first librarian of the Bollandist museum at Antwerp.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gottfried-hag:
Gottfried Hagen was town clerk of Cologne and author of the Cologne Reimchronik, or rhymed chronicle, who died in 1299.
